readings.title: The American Scholar: creative reading (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Reconcile a warning against books with a defence of reading.
readings.focus: What it means to read as an inventor.
readings.context: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882), a former Unitarian minister who settled in Concord, Massachusetts, became the best-known American lecturer and essayist of his century. Emerson gave “The American Scholar” as an address to Harvard’s Phi Beta Kappa society in August 1837. He has described the scholar as “Man Thinking” and named three influences on him: nature, books, and action. He has just warned that books revered too much produce bookworms instead of thinkers. Chaucer, Marvell and Dryden are English poets of the fourteenth to seventeenth centuries; Plato is the Greek philosopher.
readings.contentNote: This 1907 school edition keeps Emerson’s nineteenth-century habit of writing “man” and “men” for all people.

excerpt.locator: “The American Scholar,” from “Undoubtedly there is a right way of reading” to the end of the section on books; opens “Undoubtedly there is a right way of reading, so it be sternly subordinated. Man Thinking…”; closes “…colleges will recede in their public importance, whilst they grow richer every year.”.

questions.prompt: “Books are for the scholar's idle times.” When, according to the first paragraph, should a scholar read, and what does the image of the lamps suggest about what books are for?
facilitatorNotes: When “the intervals of darkness come,” when he cannot see for himself. Books are lamps lit from the sun’s ray: borrowed light that guides us back “to the East again, where the dawn is,” to our own vision. They are guides back to insight, not substitutes for it. Some readers think “idle times” undervalues books; the next paragraphs complicate it.
evidence: But when the intervals of darkness come, as come they must
we repair to the lamps which were kindled by their ray, to guide our steps to the East again, where the dawn is

questions.prompt: What explains, for Emerson, the “awe mixed with the joy” of finding that an old poet says what we had “well-nigh thought and said”?
facilitatorNotes: “The identity of all minds”: one nature wrote and the same reads. Without that doctrine, he says, we would have to imagine a “pre-established harmony,” like insects storing food for young they will never see. Students can test the experience against their own reading; some will explain it by shared human experience rather than one mind.
evidence: one nature wrote and the same reads
the philosophical doctrine of the identity of all minds

questions.prompt: “One must be an inventor to read well.” Explain “creative reading” with the help of the proverb about the wealth of the Indies.
facilitatorNotes: You bring home from a book only what you carry to it: a mind “braced by labor and invention” makes the page “luminous with manifold allusion.” Such a reader keeps only “the authentic utterances of the oracle,” even in Plato or Shakespeare. Readers may debate whether rejecting most of Shakespeare is arrogance or freedom.
evidence: He that would bring home the wealth of the Indies must carry out the wealth of the Indies.
There is then creative reading as well as creative writing.

questions.prompt: What should colleges do, according to the last paragraph, and what is Emerson’s warning to “our American colleges”? Does it still apply?
facilitatorNotes: They must teach the elements, but serve best when they aim “not to drill, but to create,” setting their students on fire. Gowns and endowments cannot replace “the least sentence or syllable of wit,” and colleges that forget this will lose importance “whilst they grow richer every year.” Students may connect the warning to schools they know, or argue that drill has a place Emerson undervalues.
evidence: they aim not to drill, but to create
our American colleges will recede in their public importance, whilst they grow richer every year

readings.title: The American Scholar: the resource to live (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow an argument that ranks living above thinking, then asks the thinker to accept loneliness.
readings.focus: Action as a resource, and the hard duties of the scholar.
readings.context: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882), a former Unitarian minister who settled in Concord, Massachusetts, became the best-known American lecturer and essayist of his century. Emerson gave “The American Scholar” as an address to Harvard’s Phi Beta Kappa society in August 1837. He has named three influences that educate the scholar, “Man Thinking”: nature, books and action, and has argued that a scholar who shuns action is less than a man. Newton’s “fits of easy transmission and reflection” described how he thought light behaves. Druids were the priests of ancient Britain and Berserkers the frenzied warriors of Norse legend; Alfred the Great was an English king. Flamsteed and Herschel were English astronomers.
readings.contentNote: This 1907 school edition keeps Emerson’s nineteenth-century habit of writing “man” and “men” for all people. Emerson calls the source of great renewers “unhandselled savage nature,” a romantic idea of the primitive.

excerpt.locator: “The American Scholar,” from the final value of action to the duties of the scholar; opens “But the final value of action, like that of books, and better than books, is that it is a…”; closes “…pronounces on the passing men and events of to-day,--this he shall hear and promulgate.”.

questions.prompt: Emerson calls action “a resource.” What does he mean, and how does the principle of “Undulation” or polarity support the claim?
facilitatorNotes: The mind alternates between thinking and acting as breath, tide, and day and night alternate. When thought runs dry the scholar can still live his truths, and living renews thinking. Polarity is “the law of nature because” it is “the law of spirit.” Some readers take action as mere refreshment for thought; the next paragraph suggests it is higher.
evidence: But the final value of action, like that of books, and better than books, is that it is a resource.
The mind now thinks, now acts, and each fit reproduces the other.

questions.prompt: “Character is higher than intellect. Thinking is the function. Living is the functionary.” What do these short sentences claim, and what limit does the end of the paragraph set on the praise of labor?
facilitatorNotes: Living is the whole act and thinking a part; a scholar shows truth by how he lives at home among those “far from fame.” Emerson welcomes the “dignity and necessity of labor” for every citizen, but on one condition: never sacrifice an opinion to popular judgment. Labor, yes; conformity, no.
evidence: Character is higher than intellect.
only be this limitation observed, that a man shall not for the sake of wider activity sacrifice any opinion to the popular judgments and modes of action

questions.prompt: Where does Emerson say “the helpful giant” comes from? What would that claim say to an audience of Harvard graduates?
facilitatorNotes: Not from those whom education has “exhausted,” but from “unhandselled savage nature,” as Alfred and Shakespeare came out of Druids and Berserkers. To Harvard men it is a provocation: their polish may be weakness. The romantic image of the “savage” as a source of vigor is a period idea worth questioning.
evidence: out of terrible Druids and Berserkers come at last Alfred and Shakespeare
What is lost in seemliness is gained in strength.

questions.prompt: Compare the astronomers Flamsteed and Herschel with the scholar “in his private observatory.” What does the scholar give up, and what “offset” does Emerson promise?
facilitatorNotes: The astronomers catalogue stars and win praise; the scholar catalogues “obscure and nebulous stars of the human mind,” unpaid, often poor and alone, at odds with “educated society.” His offset is to exercise “the highest functions of human nature,” to be “the world's eye” and “the world's heart.” Students may judge whether the offset is enough.
evidence: cataloguing obscure and nebulous stars of the human mind
He is the world's eye. He is the world's heart.

readings.title: The American Scholar: free and brave (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Trace how the most private thought becomes the most public.
readings.focus: Self-trust, courage, and Emerson’s view of “the mass.”
readings.context: Recap: Emerson has argued that action renews thought and that the scholar’s duties “may all be comprised in self-trust”: he must accept poverty and solitude to be “the world's eye” and “the world's heart.” A fetich (fetish) is an object worshipped superstitiously. Macdonald is the Scottish clan chief of the old saying; Linnæus, Davy and Cuvier were scientists who made botany, chemistry and fossils popular.
readings.contentNote: This 1907 school edition keeps Emerson’s nineteenth-century habit of writing “man” and “men” for all people. Emerson says a scholar must not expect to be protected “like children and women,” and reports history’s view of most people as “bugs” and “spawn”; the questions examine both.

excerpt.locator: “The American Scholar,” from the scholar’s self-confidence to “He lives for us, and we live in him.”; opens “These being his functions, it becomes him to feel all confidence in himself, and to defer…”; closes “…heart beat, those giant sinews combat and conquer. He lives for us, and we live in him.”.

questions.prompt: “Let him not quit his belief that a popgun is a popgun.” What public excitements does Emerson tell the scholar to ignore, and why?
facilitatorNotes: “Some fetich of a government, some ephemeral trade, or war, or man,” cried up by half the world and down by the other half: “the merest appearance.” The scholar should hold to his own patient observation. A tension follows in the next paragraph, where he condemns a scholar who hides from “politics or vexed questions”: ignore the noise, but face the danger.
evidence: Let him not quit his belief that a popgun is a popgun, though the ancient and honorable of the earth affirm it to be the crack of doom.
The world of any moment is the merest appearance.

questions.prompt: How can the most private thought prove “most public and universally true”? Use the poet and the orator to explain.
facilitatorNotes: In the secrets of his own mind the scholar finds the secrets of all minds. The poet alone records what “men in cities vast” find true; the orator finds that his “privatest, secretest presentiment” is what his hearers want, because it fulfils their own nature. The claim rests on Emerson’s belief that “man is one”; students can test it against writing that moved them.
evidence: in going down into the secrets of his own mind he has descended into the secrets of all minds
This is my music; this is myself.

questions.prompt: The scholar must be “free and brave” and not hide “like an ostrich.” What should he do with fear, and what is troubling in the phrase “like children and women”?
facilitatorNotes: Look fear in the eye, trace “the whelping of this lion” to its origin, and so see through it: “See it to be a lie, and you have already dealt it its mortal blow.” The comparison assumes women and children are a weaker, protected class, an 1837 assumption that sits oddly beside a speech about the oneness of all minds. Students may ask whose courage the address imagines.
evidence: hiding his head like an ostrich in the flowering bushes
See it to be a lie, and you have already dealt it its mortal blow.

questions.prompt: “Men are become of no account.” How does Emerson explain the devotion of “the poor and the low” to their heroes? Does he admire it or pity it?
facilitatorNotes: Both: the testimony is “full of grandeur, full of pity.” They see in the hero their own nature “ripened” and give him their dignity, which shows how great that nature is, but they also accept inferiority. Emerson wants each person to claim that dignity directly. The words “bugs” and “spawn” describe how history counts people, though some readers will hear contempt in them too.
evidence: What a testimony, full of grandeur, full of pity, is borne to the demands of his own nature
They cast the dignity of man from their downtrod selves upon the shoulders of a hero

readings.title: The American Scholar: the age of Introversion (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Weigh a defence of an anxious, self-conscious age.
readings.focus: Culture as “the upbuilding of a man,” and why a critical age need not be a sick one.
readings.context: Recap: Emerson has urged the scholar to trust himself and face his fears, and has said that the hero-worship of “the poor and the low” shows what every person might become. “The spoils of office” were government jobs handed to political supporters, a live issue under President Andrew Jackson. Etna and Vesuvius are volcanoes in Sicily and near Naples. Hamlet’s line “Sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought” describes resolve weakened by too much thinking. The American and French revolutions were within living memory.
readings.contentNote: This 1907 school edition keeps Emerson’s nineteenth-century habit of writing “man” and “men” for all people.

excerpt.locator: “The American Scholar,” from “Men such as they are very naturally seek money or power” to “This time, like all times, is a very good one”; opens “Men such as they are very naturally seek money or power; and power because it is as good…”; closes “…era? This time, like all times, is a very good one, if we but know what to do with it.”.

questions.prompt: What false good do people seek “in their sleep-walking,” and what “revolution” does Emerson expect to wake them?
facilitatorNotes: Money and power, “the spoils of office.” The revolution is “the gradual domestication of the idea of Culture,” the “upbuilding of a man,” after which people will leave government “to clerks and desks.” It is an inward revolution; students may find it hopeful or naive about politics.
evidence: This revolution is to be wrought by the gradual domestication of the idea of Culture.
The main enterprise of the world for splendor, for extent, is the upbuilding of a man.

questions.prompt: Why do we “drain all cisterns,” and why has no one ever lived “that can feed us ever”? How do the volcanoes explain it?
facilitatorNotes: Each writer shows one view of the universal mind; once we have taken it in, “we have been that man, and have passed on.” No person can contain the mind, which is “one central fire” breaking out now through Etna, now through Vesuvius: many outlets, one source. Some readers find this liberating, others think it underrates what great books keep giving.
evidence: The man has never lived that can feed us ever.
It is one central fire, which, flaming now out of the lips of Etna, lightens the capes of Sicily

questions.prompt: “Our age is bewailed as the age of Introversion.” What is the complaint, and how does Emerson answer it?
facilitatorNotes: The age is critical and self-conscious, “lined with eyes,” infected with Hamlet’s brooding. Emerson answers that “Sight is the last thing to be pitied”: seeing more is a gain, and the literary class’s discontent is a boy’s fear of water before he learns to swim. Students may ask whether Hamlet’s paralysis is dismissed too quickly.
evidence: We are lined with eyes. We see with our feet.
Sight is the last thing to be pitied.

questions.prompt: Why is an “age of Revolution” the best time to be born? Do you agree that “This time, like all times, is a very good one”?
facilitatorNotes: Old and new stand side by side and can be compared, fear and hope test everyone’s energies, and new possibilities can make up for old glories. The condition, “if we but know what to do with it,” puts the burden on the person, not the age. This is an open question, and students may test it against their own time.
evidence: when the old and the new stand side by side and admit of being compared
This time, like all times, is a very good one, if we but know what to do with it.

readings.title: The American Scholar: “We will walk on our own feet” (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Hear how an address builds to its call to action.
readings.focus: The worth of the common, the single person, and an American mind of its own.
readings.context: Recap: Emerson has argued that a critical, self-conscious age is a good time to live, “if we but know what to do with it,” and now turns to the signs of the coming days. Goldsmith, Burns, Cowper, Wordsworth and Carlyle wrote of common life; Pope, Johnson and Gibbon were polished eighteenth-century writers. Emanuel Swedenborg was a Swedish scientist and mystic; Johann Pestalozzi was a Swiss educational reformer. A firkin is a small cask.
readings.contentNote: This 1907 school edition keeps Emerson’s nineteenth-century habit of writing “man” and “men” for all people. Emerson mentions promising young men who “die of disgust, some of them suicides.”

excerpt.locator: “The American Scholar,” from the signs of the coming days to the end of the address; opens “I read with some joy of the auspicious signs of the coming days, as they glimmer already…”; closes “…because each believes himself inspired by the Divine Soul which also inspires all men.”.

questions.prompt: What is the first sign of the coming days? List some of the common things Emerson wants explained, and say what he hopes to find in them.
facilitatorNotes: Literature of the poor, the child, the street and the household; “the meal in the firkin; the milk in the pan; the ballad in the street.” He wants to see “the highest spiritual cause” in such trifles, so that one design unites “the farthest pinnacle and the lowest trench.” Readers may ask whether this honors the common for itself or only as a symbol.
evidence: I embrace the common, I explore and sit at the feet of the familiar, the low.
The meal in the firkin; the milk in the pan; the ballad in the street

questions.prompt: Why does Emerson link “the elevation of what was called the lowest class in the state” with a change in literature? What does “This writing is blood-warm” say about style?
facilitatorNotes: The democratic movement in politics has its counterpart in letters, like warm blood reaching a body’s hands and feet. Writing that attends to near things is warm; the polished style of Pope, Johnson and Gibbon looks “cold and pedantic” beside it. Style follows sympathy.
evidence: It is a sign--is it not?--of new vigor when the extremities are made active
This writing is blood-warm.

questions.prompt: “Help must come from the bosom alone.” How can setting each person apart tend “to true union”? Does Pestalozzi’s remark support Emerson or trouble him?
facilitatorNotes: People who treat each other as sovereign states meet with respect, so union of independent persons is truer than a crowd. Pestalozzi’s “melancholy” remark that no one can help another is despairing; Emerson turns it into a call to self-reliance. Some readers will find the idea bleak, or at odds with the help teachers and friends really give.
evidence: tends to true union as well as greatness
Help must come from the bosom alone.

questions.prompt: “We have listened too long to the courtly muses of Europe.” What has gone wrong with the American mind, according to the last paragraph, and what remedy does Emerson offer?
facilitatorNotes: The American spirit is “timid, imitative, tame,” avarice thickens the air, and young men of promise become drudges or die of disgust. The remedy is to plant oneself on one’s instincts and wait for the world to “come round,” refusing to be counted by party or section, “the north, or the south.” Oliver Wendell Holmes later called the address America’s “intellectual Declaration of Independence.” Students may ask whether patience is enough of a remedy.
evidence: We have listened too long to the courtly muses of Europe.
We will walk on our own feet; we will work with our own hands; we will speak our own minds.

readings.title: Self-Reliance: the sot in the duke’s bed (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Test the claim that history is “the biography of a few stout and earnest persons.”
readings.focus: Every person’s worth, and what kings and great men really teach.
readings.context: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882), a former Unitarian minister who settled in Concord, Massachusetts, became the best-known American lecturer and essayist of his century. “Self-Reliance” appeared in his Essays (1841). It has urged “Trust thyself,” declared that “Whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist,” and called a foolish consistency “the hobgoblin of little minds.” Monachism is monasticism; Antony was an early Christian hermit; George Fox founded the Quakers, John Wesley the Methodists, and Thomas Clarkson led the British campaign against the slave trade. Scanderbeg was an Albanian hero and Gustavus Adolphus a Swedish king.
readings.contentNote: This 1907 school edition keeps Emerson’s nineteenth-century habit of writing “man” and “men” for all people. Emerson likens a self-doubting person to “a charity-boy, a bastard, or an interloper.”

excerpt.locator: “Self-Reliance,” from “I hope in these days we have heard the last of conformity” to the lesson of kings; opens “I hope in these days we have heard the last of conformity and consistency. Let the words…”; closes “…signified their consciousness of their own right and comeliness, the right of every man.”.

questions.prompt: “A great man is coming to eat at my house. I do not wish to please him.” What attitude toward greatness does Emerson recommend, and how does it follow from his attack on conformity?
facilitatorNotes: Not to please but to be pleased: “I will stand here for humanity,” kind but true. Conformity means arranging oneself to please others; self-reliance makes each person “the center of things,” the measure rather than the measured. Readers may debate where self-respect ends and arrogance begins.
evidence: I do not wish to please him; I wish that he should wish to please me.
a true man belongs to no other time or place, but is the center of things

questions.prompt: “An institution is the lengthened shadow of one man.” Test this on one of Emerson’s examples. What does it explain, and what does it leave out?
facilitatorNotes: Quakerism did begin with Fox’s vision, Methodism with Wesley’s. But the claim leaves out the many who built these movements and the conditions that made them possible. “Abolition, of Clarkson” is the weakest example: it omits the enslaved who resisted and the thousands who campaigned. Students can weigh “great man” history against history from below.
evidence: An institution is the lengthened shadow of one man
all history resolves itself very easily into the biography of a few stout and earnest persons

questions.prompt: Retell the fable of the sot in the duke’s house. What does it symbolize about “the state of man”?
facilitatorNotes: A drunkard is dressed and served as a duke and told he has been mad. Emerson reverses the joke: the princely waking is the truth, and our ordinary state is the stupor. Palaces, statues and books are “suitors” awaiting our verdict. Shakespeare used the same story to open The Taming of the Shrew.
evidence: who is in the world a sort of sot, but now and then wakes up, exercises his reason, and finds himself a true prince
The picture waits for my verdict: it is not to command me

questions.prompt: If kings deserve no special deference, how has the world been “instructed by its kings”? What did the loyalty of subjects really signify?
facilitatorNotes: It was a “hieroglyphic” of people’s dim sense of “their own right and comeliness, the right of every man”: the king displayed in one person the sovereignty each person has. When private people act on original views, that luster will pass to them. Some readers find this too kind to monarchy; others see it as a democratic reading of history.
evidence: was the hieroglyphic by which they obscurely signified their consciousness of their own right and comeliness, the right of every man
When private men shall act with original views, the luster will be transferred from the actions of kings to those of gentlemen.

readings.title: Self-Reliance: “Society never advances” (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Argue with an essay that denies that progress is real.
readings.focus: The gains and losses of civilization, and the false strength of property and numbers.
readings.context: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882), a former Unitarian minister who settled in Concord, Massachusetts, became the best-known American lecturer and essayist of his century. “Self-Reliance” (1841) closes by applying self-trust to four things: prayer and creeds, travel, art, and society. Plutarch wrote lives of Greek and Roman heroes; Phocion, Anaxagoras and Diogenes were Greek statesmen and philosophers. Hudson and Bering were early explorers; Parry and Franklin led British Arctic expeditions in the 1820s. Las Casas recorded Napoleon’s conversations in exile. Ali was the fourth caliph of Islam. Whigs and Democrats were the two parties of the day.
readings.contentNote: This 1907 school edition keeps Emerson’s nineteenth-century habit of writing “man” and “men” for all people. Emerson sets “the white man” against “the naked New Zealander” and “the savage,” racial and primitivist language the questions examine.

excerpt.locator: “Self-Reliance,” the fourth application, to the end of the essay; opens “4. As our Religion, our Education, our Art look abroad, so does our spirit of society.…”; closes “…bring you peace but yourself. Nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.”.

questions.prompt: “For everything that is given, something is taken.” Which gains and losses does Emerson list? Which are convincing, and which are not?
facilitatorNotes: The coach and the lost use of the feet, the watch and the sun, the almanac and the stars, notebooks and memory, insurance and accidents, an established church and “wild virtue.” Some are persuasive (memory, attention to the sky); some are doubtful (insurance multiplying accidents). The New Zealander rests on hearsay, “If the traveler tell us truly,” and on a stereotype of the healthy savage.
evidence: The civilized man has built a coach, but has lost the use of his feet.
If the traveler tell us truly, strike the savage with a broad ax

questions.prompt: “Society is a wave.” Explain the image. How does it support the claim that “Not in time is the race progressive”?
facilitatorNotes: The wave’s form moves on, but the water only rises and falls in place; each generation dies with its experience. Great men are no greater now than in Plutarch’s day, and inventions are only “costume.” A reader can answer that knowledge, at least, accumulates; Emerson’s examples of explorers and Galileo are chosen to deny even that.
evidence: The wave moves onward, but the water of which it is composed does not.
The arts and inventions of each period are only its costume, and do not invigorate men.

questions.prompt: Why does a cultivated man become “ashamed of his property”? Distinguish “living property” from the other kind.
facilitatorNotes: Property that came by inheritance, gift or crime “has no root in him”; it stays only because no revolution or robber has taken it. Living property is what a person is and earns by being it, and it renews itself wherever he goes. Relying on property, and on governments that protect it, is “the want of self-reliance.” In a commercial society this is a sharp claim.
evidence: They measure their esteem of each other by what each has, and not by what each is.
what the man acquires is living property

questions.prompt: “He is weaker by every recruit to his banner.” What does Emerson say about conventions and numbers, and how does the last sentence sum up the essay?
facilitatorNotes: Parties and reformers gather crowds and feel stronger by “a new thousand of eyes and arms”; Emerson says strength comes from standing alone, “Is not a man better than a town?” The essay ends: peace comes only from oneself and “the triumph of principles.” Students may answer that collective action ended slavery and won votes; Emerson might reply that it began in single consciences.
evidence: It is only as a man puts off all foreign support, and stands alone, that I see him to be strong and to prevail.
Nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.

readings.title: Friendship: “the only way to have a friend is to be one” (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Follow an ideal of friendship to the point where it seems to need no friend.
readings.focus: Waiting, solitude, and love that does not ask to be returned.
readings.context: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882), a former Unitarian minister who settled in Concord, Massachusetts, became the best-known American lecturer and essayist of his century. “Friendship” appeared in his Essays (1841). Emerson has called a friend “a sort of paradox in nature,” named truth and tenderness as friendship’s two elements, and asked that a friend be “a beautiful enemy.” The numbers are the paragraph numbers of the 1907 school edition. Janus is the Roman god of doorways, with faces looking forward and back; the empyrean is the highest heaven.
readings.contentNote: This 1907 school edition keeps Emerson’s nineteenth-century habit of writing “man” and “men” for all people.

excerpt.locator: “Friendship,” paragraphs 20–24, the end of the essay; opens “20. What is so great as friendship, let us carry with what grandeur of spirit we can. Let…”; closes “…surmise or provide for infirmity. It treats its object as a god, that it may deify both.”.

questions.prompt: “Wait, and thy heart shall speak.” Why does Emerson advise silence and waiting, and what is wrong with trying to get “into his house”?
facilitatorNotes: No introductions or habits of society can make a true friendship, only “the uprise of nature in us” to the level of the other person, so that we meet “as water with water.” Hence “the only way to have a friend is to be one.” Some readers find this wise; others find it passive, or a recipe for loneliness.
evidence: the only way to have a friend is to be one
You shall not come nearer a man by getting into his house.

questions.prompt: “I do then with my friends as I do with my books.” What does Emerson want from his friends, and why can he not “afford” to talk with them?
facilitatorNotes: He wants them near but seldom used, and fears that talk will make him lose his own “presentiments,” his “spiritual astronomy.” He will take “not what they have, but what they are.” Many readers find this cold; others see a respect that will not use friends up.
evidence: I would have them where I can find them, but I seldom use them.
I will receive from them, not what they have, but what they are.

questions.prompt: Emerson imagines saying even to the dearest friends, “Who are you? Unhand me.” How can parting make friends “more each other's”?
facilitatorNotes: By making each more his own: they “part only to meet again on a higher platform.” A friend is “Janus-faced,” child of the past and “harbinger of a greater friend.” Students can decide whether this describes friendship or self-development using friends along the way.
evidence: thus we part only to meet again on a higher platform, and only be more each other's, because we are more our own
A friend is Janus-faced

questions.prompt: In the last paragraph, can love be “unrequited”? How do the essay’s final sentences turn back on what Emerson has just said?
facilitatorNotes: True love “transcends the unworthy object,” as the sun does not mind the rays lost in space. Then he catches himself: to plan for a friend’s failure is “a sort of treachery,” because friendship’s essence is “entireness,” a trust that does not provide for weakness. The essay ends in a tension it does not resolve.
evidence: Yet these things may hardly be said without a sort of treachery to the relation.
It treats its object as a god, that it may deify both.

readings.title: Heroism: “a tart cathartic virtue” (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Read a quoted play scene as evidence in an essay.
readings.focus: What heroic literature is for, and why a person must be armed for a world at war.
readings.context: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882), a former Unitarian minister who settled in Concord, Massachusetts, became the best-known American lecturer and essayist of his century. “Heroism” appeared in his Essays (1841). The epigraph is a saying attributed to the Prophet Muhammad (“Mahomet” in older English). Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher were English playwrights of the early 1600s; in the scene Emerson quotes from their collected plays, the Roman general Martius has conquered Athens and ordered the death of its duke, Sophocles. Ariadne’s crown is a constellation. Plutarch wrote lives of Greek and Roman heroes; Thomas Carlyle published On Heroes and Hero-Worship in 1841. A gibbet is a gallows.
readings.contentNote: This 1907 school edition keeps Emerson’s nineteenth-century habit of writing “man” and “men” for all people. The scene is an execution. Emerson says that noble birth showed in the old plays “as color is in our American population,” a racial comparison of his time, and lists disease and madness as punishments of nature.

excerpt.locator: “Heroism,” the epigraph and paragraphs 1–4, with the scene Emerson quotes from Beaumont and Fletcher; opens “"Paradise is under the shadow of swords," _Mahomet._”; closes “…and the mob by the absolute truth of his speech, and the rectitude of his behavior.”.

questions.prompt: Why quote the scene at such length? What makes Sophocles heroic, and what does his conduct do to his conqueror?
facilitatorNotes: He will not beg for his life, refuses a long farewell, says that “to die / Is to begin to live,” and kneels with his back to his killer. His “disdain of fortune and of death” conquers Martius, who spares him: “he is free, / And Martius walks now in captivity.” The quotation shows the “heroic cast” instead of describing it; Dorigen’s courage is part of the scene too.
evidence: Thou now hast found a way to conquer me.
Then we have vanquished nothing; he is free, And Martius walks now in captivity.

questions.prompt: What kind of writing does Emerson miss in his own day, and where does he find it? What does the contrast of “flutes and flageolets” with the “fife” suggest?
facilitatorNotes: The press of his day plays soft pipes; the fife is martial and rousing. He finds the note in a few modern works (Wordsworth, Scott, Carlyle, Burns) and above all in Plutarch, “its Doctor and historian,” whose courage is “a Stoicism not of the schools, but of the blood.” Students may ask what heroic writing looks like now.
evidence: We have a great many flutes and flageolets, but not often the sound of any fife.
A wild courage, a Stoicism not of the schools, but of the blood

questions.prompt: Why, according to paragraph 3, do we need “books of this tart cathartic virtue”? How does Emerson explain suffering?
facilitatorNotes: Life looks dangerous from “the nook and chimney-side of prudence”: disease, war, plague and famine show “a certain ferocity in nature,” which came in by human wrongdoing and goes out through suffering, so everyone is “a stockholder in the sin.” Books of courage purge fear. Students may question the idea that illness is punishment for broken laws, a moral view of disease common in his time.
evidence: Life is a festival only to the wise.
almost no man exists who has not in his own person become, to some amount, a stockholder in the sin

questions.prompt: “He is born into the state of war.” What war does paragraph 4 mean, and what weapons does Emerson’s hero carry?
facilitatorNotes: Not a battlefield but a moral struggle with the gibbet and the mob; the weapons are “the absolute truth of his speech, and the rectitude of his behavior,” carried “with perfect urbanity.” Heroism here is moral courage. Readers may ask whether the military language, and the epigraph about swords, glorifies violence or redirects it.
evidence: Our culture, therefore, must not omit the arming of the man.
dare the gibbet and the mob by the absolute truth of his speech, and the rectitude of his behavior
